section.title: The Two Eagles and the Vine
section.sectionRationale: Ezekiel is told to pose a riddle rather than simply announce judgment: a great eagle plants a vine that then bends toward a second eagle for water, a veiled picture of King Zedekiah's sworn covenant with Babylon and his treacherous reach for help from Egypt. The riddle is unlocked in plain language, judgment is pronounced, and then the chapter turns unexpectedly toward hope: God Himself will plant a tender shoot that grows into a sheltering, messianic cedar.
section.thesis: God exposes Zedekiah's broken oath to Babylon as treason against Himself, since the covenant had been sworn in His name, and though the failed king's own scheming brings him to ruin, the LORD promises to plant His own tender shoot on Zion, a kingdom that will grow from humble beginnings into a shelter for every nation, fulfilled in Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: a great eagle plants a low, dependent vine; a second eagle to whom the vine treacherously turns for water; the riddle unlocked as Zedekiah's broken covenant with Babylon and his betrayal to Egypt; and God's own counter-promise, a tender shoot planted into a majestic, messianic cedar.

units.label: A great eagle plants a vine

verses.text: Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, pose a {{chidah|riddle}}; speak a parable to the house of Israel
and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘A great {{nesher|eagle}} with great wings and long pinions, full of feathers of many colors, came to Lebanon and took away the top of the cedar.
He plucked off its topmost shoot, carried it to the land of merchants, and planted it in a city of traders.
He took some of the seed of the land and planted it in fertile soil; he placed it by abundant waters and set it out like a willow.
It sprouted and became a spreading vine, low in height, with branches turned toward him; yet its roots remained where it stood. So it became a vine and yielded branches and sent out shoots.

units.label: A second eagle, and a vine that turns
units.note: the vine bends toward Egypt instead of trusting its planter

verses.text: But there was another great eagle with great wings and many feathers. And behold, this vine bent its roots toward him. It stretched out its branches to him from its planting bed, so that he might water it.
It had been planted in good soil by abundant waters in order to yield branches and bear fruit and become a splendid vine.’

So you are to tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Will it flourish? Will it not be uprooted and stripped of its fruit so that it shrivels? All its foliage will wither! It will not take a strong arm or many people to pull it up by its roots.
Even if it is transplanted, will it flourish? Will it not completely wither when the east wind strikes? It will wither on the bed where it sprouted.’”

units.label: The riddle unlocked, a broken oath
units.note: Zedekiah's covenant with Babylon and betrayal to Egypt

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

“Now say to this rebellious house: ‘Do you not know what these things mean?’ Tell them, ‘Behold, the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, carried off its king and officials, and brought them back with him to Babylon.
He took a member of the royal family and made a {{berit|covenant}} with him, putting him under oath. Then he carried away the leading men of the land,
so that the kingdom would be brought low, unable to lift itself up, surviving only by keeping his covenant.

But this king rebelled against Babylon by sending his envoys to Egypt to ask for horses and a large army. Will he flourish? Will the one who does such things escape? Can he break a covenant and yet escape?’
‘As surely as I live,’ declares the Lord GOD, ‘he will die in Babylon, in the land of the king who enthroned him, whose oath he despised and whose covenant he broke.
Pharaoh with his mighty army and vast horde will not help him in battle, when ramps are built and siege walls constructed to destroy many lives.
He despised the oath by breaking the covenant. Seeing that he gave his hand in pledge yet did all these things, he will not escape!’
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘As surely as I live, I will bring down upon his head My oath that he despised and My covenant that he broke.
I will spread My net over him and catch him in My snare. I will bring him to Babylon and execute judgment upon him there for the treason he committed against Me.
All his choice troops will fall by the sword, and those who survive will be scattered to every wind. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken.’

units.label: The tender shoot of the LORD's planting
units.note: a messianic promise of a kingdom to come

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar, and I will set it out. I will pluck a {{yoneqet|tender sprig}} from its topmost shoots, and I will plant it on a high and lofty mountain.

I will plant it on the mountain heights of Israel so that it will bear branches; it will yield fruit and become a majestic cedar. Birds of every kind will nest under it, taking shelter in the shade of its branches.

Then all the trees of the field will know that I am the LORD. I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall. I dry up the green tree and make the withered tree flourish. I, the LORD, have spoken, and I have done it.’”

chidah.gloss: A riddle or dark saying, a puzzle to be pondered before its meaning is unlocked. Ezekiel is told to pose a riddle rather than state Judah's judgment plainly, so that the house of Israel must reckon with the truth for themselves before it is spelled out in verses 11 to 21.

nesher.gloss: Eagle, a common ancient image for a great king or empire swooping down in conquest. The first eagle pictures Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon; the second, introduced in verse 7, pictures Pharaoh of Egypt, to whom Judah foolishly turned instead of trusting the covenant it had sworn.

berit.gloss: Covenant, here the vassal treaty Zedekiah swore to Nebuchadnezzar in the LORD's name, 2 Chronicles 36:13. Breaking it was not merely political treachery but, in Ezekiel's theology, treason against God Himself, since the oath had been sworn by His name.

yoneqet.gloss: A tender shoot or young twig, easily overlooked beside the 'lofty top' from which it is taken. God's promised king grows not from human scheming, like Zedekiah's failed diplomacy, but from God's own quiet planting, a pattern Isaiah and the Gospels apply to the Messiah's humble, surprising rise.

basic.context: This chapter follows Ezekiel's sign-acts and oracles of judgment with a riddle-parable aimed at 'this rebellious house'. Judah's king Zedekiah, installed as Babylon's vassal and bound by a sworn covenant, secretly appealed to Egypt for military help, breaking his oath. The parable of two eagles and a vine exposes this betrayal, and ends with a surprising counter-promise: God Himself will plant a tender shoot that grows into a sheltering, majestic cedar.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a riddle, a mashal, deliberately puzzling until Ezekiel unlocks it himself in verses 11 to 21: the first eagle is Nebuchadnezzar, the vine is Zedekiah, the second eagle is Egypt. The historical betrayal is real and the judgment concrete, but the closing image of the tender shoot reaches beyond the immediate political crisis to a promise that outlasts it.
basic.originalLanguages: Ezekiel poses a chidah, a riddle, whose two nesher, eagles, and bent vine picture Judah's fatal reach for Egypt after swearing a berit, covenant, to Babylon in the LORD's name. The chapter turns on a yoneqet, a tender and easily overlooked shoot, which God Himself will plant into a majestic, sheltering cedar.
basic.typology: The tender shoot planted on a high mountain that grows into a cedar sheltering birds of every kind anticipates Christ's kingdom: small and unimpressive in its beginnings, as in the parable of the mustard seed, yet becoming a refuge for every nation.
basic.christ: Ezekiel 17:22-24 promises that God, not human scheming, will plant a tender shoot from the cedar's lofty top onto Israel's mountain heights, where it becomes a majestic tree sheltering birds of every kind. This is echoed in Isaiah's shoot from the stump of Jesse, 11:1, Jeremiah's righteous Branch, 23:5, and Jesus' parable of the mustard seed becoming a tree in whose branches birds can nest, Matthew 13:31-32, His kingdom growing from humble, hidden beginnings into a shelter for every people.
basic.god: God exposes political treachery for what it is, treason against Himself, since Zedekiah's broken treaty had been sworn in the LORD's name; His justice topples the proud schemer who trusted Egypt over his own sworn word. Yet the same God who judges Zedekiah's failed self-rescue announces His own rescue plan, planting a king by His own hand rather than leaving the Davidic line's future to human intrigue.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 11:1-10 promises a shoot from Jesse's stump bearing the Spirit's fullness. Jeremiah 23:5-6 promises a righteous Branch to reign as David's true heir. Matthew 13:31-32 pictures the kingdom of heaven as a mustard seed growing into a tree where birds nest, echoing this chapter's image directly. 2 Kings 24:17-20 and 2 Chronicles 36:11-13 record Zedekiah's historical installation and broken oath.
basic.oneStory: This is the story of a king who broke his sworn word chasing a human rescue that could never hold, and the God who answers not with abandonment but with His own planting, a tender shoot who becomes a sheltering kingdom, tracing a straight line to Jesus, the Branch in whom every nation finds a home.

context.literary:
The chapter moves in three beats, and the third deliberately answers the first. Verses 1 to 10 give the riddle and parable, verses 11 to 21 unlock it, and verses 22 to 24 offer a second, shorter parable in which the eagles disappear and God speaks in the first person. Notice how the opening act is mirrored. In verses 3 and 4 the great eagle 'took away the top of the cedar' and 'plucked off its topmost shoot.' In verse 22 the LORD says, 'I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar' and 'I will pluck a tender sprig from its topmost shoots.' The same cedar, the same crown, the same verb of plucking, but now in the hand of God and bound for a mountain instead of a city of traders. What the empire did to the royal house, God will undo and redo on His own terms.

The riddle also teaches by its small details. The vine is 'low in height' and spreading, set 'like a willow' by abundant water, verses 5 and 6. This was never meant to be a towering cedar. Its whole calling was to lean toward the one who planted it and to live. The sin of the second half is therefore a sin of posture: the vine bends its roots and branches toward a second eagle, verse 7. Three rhetorical questions then close off every hope, 'Will it flourish?' in verses 9, 10 and 15, each expecting the answer no, until the same word 'flourish' becomes a promise in verses 23 and 24.

The chapter sits inside a run of images. Chapter 15 spoke of the vine as useless wood, chapter 16 of an unfaithful bride, and chapter 17 now turns to a political betrayal. The decoding passage begins with a sharp question, 'Do you not know what these things mean?', verse 12, which tells us the audience was expected to be able to read the image if they had been listening.
context.historical:
Ezekiel was among those carried off with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, Ezekiel 1:2, and he speaks to fellow exiles who hoped the exile would be short. Nebuchadnezzar had left Jerusalem a vassal king. He took Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah, changed his name to Zedekiah and put him on the throne, 2 Kings 24:17, and he made him swear loyalty by God, 2 Chronicles 36:13. That detail matters. In the ancient Near East a treaty was sealed with an oath before the gods, and a broken treaty was a crime against the gods who had witnessed it. Zedekiah had invoked the LORD, so his rebellion was aimed at the LORD, not only at Babylon.

Pressure to rebel was strong. Envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon came to Jerusalem early in his reign, Jeremiah 27:1-3, and false prophets promised a quick return of the exiles. Jeremiah answered with a yoke on his neck and the counsel to serve Babylon and live, Jeremiah 27:12. Egypt was the hoped-for rescuer. Horses were the very thing a king of Israel was warned not to chase back to Egypt, Deuteronomy 17:16, and Isaiah had mocked the same instinct, Isaiah 31:1.

The outcome was exactly as spoken. When a relief army from Egypt appeared, it turned back, Jeremiah 37:5-7. Zedekiah was overtaken on the plains of Jericho, brought to Riblah, made to watch his sons killed, blinded and taken to Babylon, 2 Kings 25:4-7 and Jeremiah 52:8-11. Ezekiel had said he would be brought to Babylon yet 'not see it,' Ezekiel 12:13, a riddle of its own that the blinding explains.
context.canonical:
Trees stand for kingdoms across the Bible. Ezekiel himself pictures Assyria as a cedar where 'all the birds of the air nested in its branches,' Ezekiel 31:6, and Daniel sees Nebuchadnezzar as a great tree under which the beasts shelter and in whose branches the birds nest, Daniel 4:12. Those trees are all brought down. Ezekiel 17:22 to 24 is different because God plants the tree Himself, and it is a tree for the humble. The idea of the LORD planting His people on a mountain goes back to the exodus song, 'You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance,' Exodus 15:17.

The vine imagery runs from Psalm 80 and Isaiah 5 through Ezekiel 15 and 19, always with the sad verdict that Israel as God's vine failed. The royal hope runs on a parallel track. After the cedar is cut, Isaiah promises 'a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse,' Isaiah 11:1, and Jeremiah a righteous Branch, Jeremiah 23:5. Zechariah names the Branch outright, Zechariah 6:12.

The sanctity of an oath has its own canonical line. Israel kept a sworn promise to the Gibeonites even though it had been won by trickery, Joshua 9:18-20, and when Saul later struck at them God sent famine, 2 Samuel 21:1-2. The Lord reverses the proud and lifts the low, a pattern Hannah sings, 1 Samuel 2:7-8, Mary echoes, Luke 1:52, and Jesus turns into the parable of the mustard seed, Mark 4:31-32.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wanted the exiles to stop reading Zedekiah's rebellion as patriotism. A people in Babylon longed to hear that their king was about to break the yoke, and a clever riddle let them hear the truth in their own time. He wanted them to see that the issue was not Babylon's power but an oath sworn in the LORD's name, which Zedekiah had treated as disposable, verses 16 to 19.

He also wanted them to see that political cleverness cannot save a vine that has lost its root. Sending envoys for horses and an army, verse 15, looks like strength and is in fact withering. The east wind will dry it on the very bed where it sprouted, verse 10.

But the chapter does not end in judgment. The last three verses were meant to give the exiles something to hold. The royal line is cut, but God has kept the crown of the cedar in His own hand, and He will plant what He chooses where He chooses. The hearers were to stop trusting Egypt and stop trusting Babylon, and wait on the God who both brings down and raises up, verse 24.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a particular king's perjury and its consequences. It does not hand later readers a rule that every government must be obeyed whatever it commands, nor a rule that rebellion is always sin. Elsewhere Scripture honours those who refuse a ruler's command to disobey God, as in Daniel 3 and Acts 5:29. What carries across is the narrower principle: a promise made in God's name is heard by God, and a believer who gives his word to a hostile or unbelieving party is still bound by it.

The riddle's final promise is likewise a prophecy rather than a template. Believers are not told to plant anything. They are told that the God who makes the low tree tall chooses small beginnings, so that the small, hidden and unimpressive things of His kingdom should not be despised.

debates.question: Was Zedekiah's oath to Babylon binding even though it was forced on him?

views.label: Yes, because it was sworn in God's name
views.case: God calls the oath 'My oath' and the covenant 'My covenant,' verse 19, and treats the breach as treason against Himself, verse 20. On this reading the circumstances of the oath do not weaken it; a promise made before God binds the one who made it, as Israel's oath to the Gibeonites bound them, Joshua 9:18-20.

views.label: Yes, and the real fault lay in the Egyptian scheme as well
views.case: Others stress that Zedekiah's sin was twofold: he broke faith, and he looked to Egypt for rescue instead of to the LORD, verse 15. Jeremiah's counsel to serve Babylon and live, Jeremiah 27:12, gave him a path of humble obedience that he refused.

views.label: The text condemns the perjury but does not bless Babylon's rule
views.case: A third view cautions that Ezekiel never says Nebuchadnezzar's demand was just. The point is that Zedekiah called on God to witness and then lied, whatever the character of the treaty. Babylon is later judged for its own pride, so the passage does not turn every imperial treaty into divine law.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the heart is the same: God holds a person to the word he gave in His name. The passage is a warning against casual oaths and against solving a political problem by breaking faith.

debates.question: What is the 'tender sprig' of verses 22 to 24?

views.label: A descendant of David restored in the near term
views.case: The shoot is plucked from the same top of the cedar that the eagle took in verse 4, so it must be of the royal line. Some see in it the hope that the Davidic house would be re-established after exile, as with Jehoiachin's release, 2 Kings 25:27-30, or Zerubbabel.

views.label: The Messiah, Jesus Christ
views.case: A mountain where birds of every kind nest, a tree that lifts up the lowly, and a kingdom planted by God's own hand exceed what any post-exilic governor achieved. Jewish and Christian readers alike have long taken the shoot as the Messiah, and Jesus' parable of the mustard seed seems to draw on the image, Mark 4:31-32.

views.label: Both, in stages
views.case: Many hold that the promise has a layered fulfilment: the royal line survives exile in the near term, and the great tree appears finally in Christ and His kingdom.

debates.bearing: The text itself names no individual, so the first hearers heard a promise that the cut-down royal house would live. The New Testament shows who is the one in whom that promise comes true.

study.originalLanguages:
Ezekiel is told to 'pose a riddle,' verse 2, using chidah, the word of Samson's riddle in Judges 14:12 and of the 'riddles of the wise' in Proverbs 1:6. A chidah hides its meaning on purpose, and the prophet's job is partly to withhold and then reveal. He is also to speak a mashal, a parable, which is the broader word for any comparison or proverb. The two terms together warn that the surface story, birds and plants, is not the point.

The eagle, nesher, is a strange choice because the LORD Himself had once said He carried Israel 'on eagles' wings,' Exodus 19:4. Here two great birds of prey, Babylon and Egypt, take that role of carrier and planter. Neither is the real protector, and the vine learns the difference too late.

The word for the oath in verses 13, 16, 18 and 19 is alah, and the word for covenant is berit. In verse 19 God claims both with a possessive, 'My oath' and 'My covenant.' The verb 'despised,' bazah, repeats in verses 16, 18 and 19, and the verb of breaking a covenant, parar, is the standard biblical term for covenant violation. The vine 'gave his hand in pledge,' verse 18, which is the gesture of handshake agreement, as in 2 Kings 10:15. The final verdict is 'treason' in verse 20, from the root ma'al, a word normally used of a breach of faith against holy things, as in Joshua 7:1. Perjury in God's name is put in the category of sacrilege.

In verse 13 the BSB footnote notes that Hebrew has 'the royal seed.' In verse 5 the footnote shows the Hebrew 'in a field of seed.' The word zera, seed, is in both places, and it ties the planted shoot to the royal line of David.

The word for 'tender sprig' in verse 22, yoneqet, comes from the root that gives the 'tender shoot' of Isaiah 53:2, where a different form of the same word describes the servant. Verse 4 had 'topmost shoot' and verse 22 'topmost shoots,' the same word, the same plucking verb, and the added adjective 'tender' to make the point that God's chosen king would be soft and small at the outset. The east wind of verse 10 is the scorching wind from the desert side, a stock image of judgment, Hosea 13:15.

Verse 20 repeats almost word for word the 'net' and 'snare' of Ezekiel 12:13. The hunting image is the same, and the later oracle explains the earlier.

typology.type: The tender sprig planted on a high mountain, Ezekiel 17:22-23
typology.fulfillment: A cut-down royal house yields one small shoot that God plants and that grows into a majestic tree. Isaiah speaks of the servant who 'grew up before Him like a tender shoot,' Isaiah 53:2, and Jesus is born of David's line in a small town and a stable. The type escalates in Christ because He is not merely a restored king but the Branch who builds the temple, Zechariah 6:12, and reigns over every nation. Where Zedekiah was planted by a conqueror and withered, Christ is planted by the Father and will not.

typology.type: Birds of every kind nesting under the tree, Ezekiel 17:23
typology.fulfillment: Nations that once sheltered under Assyria's cedar and Nebuchadnezzar's tree, Ezekiel 31:6 and Daniel 4:12, now find shelter under God's own tree. Jesus takes the image for the kingdom of heaven, a seed that grows 'so that the birds of the air nest in its shade,' Mark 4:32. The kingdom is the true refuge for peoples of every origin, Revelation 7:9. The type falls short only in that it is a picture of Israel's land; in Christ the shelter is not bound to a mountain in Judah, for His people come from every nation.

typology.type: Zedekiah the broken oath, contrasted with the faithful king, Ezekiel 17:15-19
typology.fulfillment: Zedekiah is a negative type: a son of David who swore and then lied. The letter to the Hebrews presents Jesus as the one who 'has become the guarantee of a better covenant' by an oath of God, Hebrews 7:22. Where Zedekiah despised the oath, Jesus became obedient to death, Philippians 2:8, and keeps every promise made to David, Psalm 89:34-35. The contrast is complete, and it shows what a Davidic king was supposed to be. The correspondence is by contrast, not by likeness.

typology.type: The proud tree made low and the low tree made tall, Ezekiel 17:24
typology.fulfillment: God's pattern of reversal governs the chapter and reaches its fullest form in the cross and resurrection. Christ, who was in the form of God, emptied Himself and was then highly exalted, Philippians 2:6-9, and Mary sang that He has 'brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble,' Luke 1:52. The type is a principle rather than a single event; it is applied in Christ as the supreme case, and it shapes the lives of His followers, who are told to expect exaltation through humility, Matthew 23:12.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ through the royal line, the planting and the reversal. First, the line. The eagle in verse 4 took the very top of the cedar, and the shoot God promises in verse 22 comes from that same top. The Davidic house had been cut, Jehoiachin carried away and Zedekiah destined for ruin, but the promise is that the line itself is not abandoned. Matthew's genealogy runs straight through the exile, naming Jeconiah 'at the time of the exile to Babylon,' Matthew 1:11, and arrives at Jesus. Isaiah speaks of a shoot from the stump of Jesse, Isaiah 11:1, and Jeremiah of a righteous Branch who 'will reign wisely as King,' Jeremiah 23:5. Ezekiel 17 is one of those promises from the exile that the line is cut but not dead.

Second, the planting. In the riddle every planter is a human power, a conqueror or a pharaoh. In the promise the planter is God, and He plants on 'a high and lofty mountain,' which in Ezekiel's world means Zion. The kingdom of Christ is exactly this kind of kingdom, one not founded by armies. Jesus said His kingdom is not of this world, John 18:36, and He taught it by saying it begins as the smallest seed and becomes a plant in whose shade the birds nest, Mark 4:31-32. The echo of Ezekiel 17:23 is unmistakable. Notice the deliberate change: Ezekiel's tree is a majestic cedar, but Jesus picks a garden plant, a mustard, so that the kingdom's glory is not that of an empire. Its greatness is shelter, not domination.

Third, the contrast. Zedekiah is everything a Davidic king should not be: he took an oath in God's name and called it nothing. Jesus is the one who kept every word, 'obedient to death,' Philippians 2:8, and who guarantees a better covenant, Hebrews 7:22. The vine of Judah leaned its roots toward Egypt; Jesus says, 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1, the one whose roots never bend away from His Father.

Fourth, the reversal. Verse 24 says God makes the low tree tall and the withered tree flourish. This is the shape of the gospel. The one who 'had no stately form or majesty,' Isaiah 53:2, was lifted up and given the name above every name, Philippians 2:9. And those joined to Him share it: 'whoever humbles himself will be exalted,' Matthew 23:12.

A caution is needed. Ezekiel 17:22 to 24 never says 'Messiah,' and not every feature of the tree is a code for Jesus. The link is made by the whole prophetic stream that takes up the shoot and the Branch, and by Jesus' own use of the tree image. What this chapter supplies is a promise that God will not leave the throne of David to Zedekiah's kind, and the New Testament names the one who fills it.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who takes oaths personally. He says 'My oath' and 'My covenant,' verse 19, as though the promise Zedekiah swore to a pagan king had been sworn to Him, and in a real sense it had, because He was invoked as witness. Nothing in Scripture suggests that God cares only about promises made between believers. He enforced Israel's oath to the Gibeonites, 2 Samuel 21:1-2, and He holds a Judean king to a promise made to Babylon. The God of this passage is a God of truthfulness, and He expects the people who bear His name to be people whose word means something.

It also shows God's rule over empires without making Him the author of sin. Nebuchadnezzar enthroned Zedekiah and could be called an instrument, yet Zedekiah is judged for his own decision to break faith and to trust Egypt. God does not ask the exiles to resolve how both are true. He lets Zedekiah's choices run their course, and the net He spreads is the consequence of the king's own scheming, verse 20. Egypt cannot help, verse 17, and Jeremiah records that the Egyptian army went home, Jeremiah 37:7.

The passage shows a God who is both the demolisher and the gardener. Verse 24 holds the two together: 'I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall. I dry up the green tree and make the withered tree flourish.' The same sovereign hand that withers Zedekiah plants the new shoot. His justice and His mercy are not at war here; the humbling of the proud makes room for the lifting of the low, as Hannah had sung, 1 Samuel 2:7-8.

God is also faithful to a promise that Judah's kings could not keep. He had sworn 'I will not violate My covenant,' Psalm 89:34, and Ezekiel 17 is the exiles' assurance that Zedekiah's treachery did not cancel God's own oath to David. When the vine fails, God does not withdraw; He begins again with a sprig.

Finally, the final verse is a signature: 'I, the LORD, have spoken, and I have done it.' His word and His act are one. For worship, this means the people of God can stop trusting in horses and treaties and bring their anxious schemes to the One whose planting does not wither. It also means we should be very slow with our promises, and very quick to keep them.

crossReferences.note: The historical record of Zedekiah's appointment by Nebuchadnezzar, his change of name from Mattaniah, and his rebellion. It confirms that the king in the riddle is a real man placed on the throne by Babylon, and that his revolt was the cause of the final siege of Jerusalem.

Adds the key detail that Nebuchadnezzar 'had made him swear by God.' This is why Ezekiel can call the broken treaty treason against the LORD, and why the Chronicler says Zedekiah stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD.

Jeremiah's message to the same king, in the same years: put your necks under the yoke of Babylon, serve and live. Read with Ezekiel 17, it shows that the two prophets, one in Jerusalem and one in exile, gave the same counsel, and that Zedekiah had been told plainly what to do.

The Egyptian army marches out to help, and the LORD says it will go back to its own land. This is the fulfilment of verse 17, where Pharaoh with his mighty army will not help Zedekiah in battle. The hope the king put in horses proved empty.

An earlier oracle already said that the prince would be caught in God's net and brought to Babylon, 'yet he will not see it.' Ezekiel 17:20 repeats the net and the snare, and the blinding at Riblah, 2 Kings 25:7, resolves what looked like a contradiction.

Assyria is pictured as a cedar of Lebanon with birds nesting in its branches and nations living in its shade. Set beside Ezekiel 17:23, it shows that the shelter image is a standard picture of imperial greatness, and that God's own tree is a rival, humble kingdom that outlasts every empire.

Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree that gave shelter and food to every creature, and then of its being cut down. The same image of an overshadowing tree is used for the king who enthroned Zedekiah, which shows how fully God overrules the empire that Judah feared.

The servant 'grew up before Him like a tender shoot, and like a root out of dry ground.' The word for a tender shoot comes from the same root as Ezekiel's tender sprig. It shows that the humble beginning of God's chosen king is part of the prophetic pattern, not an accident.

A man whose name is the Branch will 'branch out from His place and build the temple of the LORD.' The Branch is now explicitly a person and a builder. Ezekiel's tender sprig and Zechariah's Branch speak of one hope that finally takes the form of Jesus.

Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a mustard seed that grows into the largest of garden plants, with birds nesting in its shade. He quietly shifts the image from a majestic cedar to a humble garden plant, and so shows that the greatness of the kingdom is in its shelter, not its show.

Mary's song says God 'has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble.' It is the doctrine of Ezekiel 17:24 sung by the mother of the Messiah, and it announces that the reversal long promised is about to be accomplished in her Son.

study.oneStory:
Genesis opens with God planting a garden, Genesis 2:8, and its story is soon one of broken covenant, 'like Adam, have transgressed the covenant,' Hosea 6:7. Israel was then planted by God on the mountain of His inheritance, Exodus 15:17, and was meant to be a fruitful vine. Ezekiel 17 reads the tragic end of that experiment in the person of its last king: a vine that was set in good soil and still turned away. The oath was broken, the roots were pulled, and the east wind came.

But Ezekiel will not let the story close there. The cut cedar becomes the first sign that God Himself would plant again. This is the pivot between the failure of Israel's kings and the hope of one king who would not fail. After the exile the line runs through Jehoiachin and Zerubbabel, and Haggai even called Zerubbabel a signet ring, Haggai 2:23, but no governor could fill the picture of a majestic cedar sheltering every kind of bird. The promise waited for Jesus.

In the Gospels the shoot appears as a baby in a small town, the mustard seed buried and rising, the vine whose branches bear fruit for the Father. The kingdom grows without the swords and treaties that Zedekiah trusted. After the resurrection the shelter spreads outward and receives people from every nation, which is the way the birds of verse 23 come to the tree.

The new creation brings the story to its goal. Daniel's stone becomes a mountain that fills the earth, Daniel 2:35, and John sees at the centre of the city the tree of life, whose leaves 'are for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2. The planting of God has become a garden city, and the shelter promised to the exiles is the shelter of all who are His. Every proud tree has been brought down. The one tree that stands was planted by God and bears fruit all year.

For the reader today, the chapter places Zedekiah's story within the great sweep. We are tempted to make our own treaties with Egypt, to rescue ourselves by our own cleverness. Ezekiel 17 invites us instead to be the low vine, rooted and bending toward the one who planted us, and to wait for the God who makes the low tree tall.

quiz.q: What does the first eagle do to the cedar in Ezekiel's riddle, and what does it represent?

options.text: It destroys the whole cedar, leaving nothing standing.
options.note: Only the topmost shoot is plucked away, not the whole tree; the picture is deportation of the royal house, not total destruction.

options.text: It plucks off the cedar's topmost shoot and plants it in a city of traders, picturing Nebuchadnezzar carrying off Judah's king to Babylon.
options.note: Verses 3-4 and 12 confirm this exactly, the first eagle acting for Babylon.

options.text: It waters the cedar so it grows taller than before.
options.note: The eagle removes the shoot and carries it away; it does not nourish the cedar in place.

options.text: It ignores the cedar entirely and flies elsewhere.
options.note: The eagle is deeply involved, plucking and transplanting the shoot; it does not merely pass by.

quiz.q: What does the transplanted vine do when a second eagle appears?

options.text: It stays rooted only toward the one who first planted it, refusing the second eagle.
options.note: The opposite happens; the vine bends its roots and branches toward the second eagle.

options.text: It bends its roots and stretches its branches toward the second eagle, seeking water it did not need.
options.note: Verse 7 states this plainly, even though verse 8 notes it was already planted by abundant waters.

options.text: It withers immediately without any explanation given.
options.note: Withering is announced only later, in verses 9-10, as the coming judgment for this disloyalty.

options.text: It grows a little toward the second eagle but mostly remains unaffected.
options.note: The text describes a decisive, full turning of roots and branches, not a slight or partial shift.

quiz.q: According to the riddle's explanation in verses 12-15, what did Judah's king do that provoked judgment?

options.text: He kept his sworn covenant with Babylon faithfully throughout his reign.
options.note: The text says the opposite; he despised the oath and broke the covenant.

options.text: He simply grew old and died a natural death in Jerusalem.
options.note: Verse 16 specifies he would die in Babylon, not naturally in Jerusalem, as judgment for his betrayal.

options.text: He rebelled against Babylon by sending envoys to Egypt for horses and a large army, breaking his sworn covenant.
options.note: Verse 15 states this directly, and verses 18-19 identify it as breaking a covenant sworn in the LORD's name.

options.text: He rebelled against Babylon but never sought any foreign alliance.
options.note: His rebellion specifically involved seeking Egypt's military help, not standing alone.

quiz.q: Why does God treat the breaking of Zedekiah's political treaty with Babylon as treason against Himself?

options.text: Because political treaties always carry automatic religious weight regardless of how they are sworn.
options.note: The text specifies the reason as the oath being sworn in the LORD's name, not treaties in general.

options.text: Because the treaty happened to be signed inside the temple courts.
options.note: No such detail about the temple appears in this chapter's account of the covenant.

options.text: Because the covenant and oath had been sworn in the LORD's own name, so breaking it despised Him personally.
options.note: Verses 18-19 make this explicit: 'My oath that he despised and My covenant that he broke.'

options.text: Because Babylon was itself a worshiper of the LORD and deserved special loyalty.
options.note: Babylon's own religious status is not the point; the oath's connection to the LORD's name is what makes betrayal treasonous.

quiz.q: What does God promise to do in the chapter's closing verses, 17:22-24?

options.text: Leave the Davidic line permanently ended with no future planting or restoration.
options.note: The chapter's very point is a promised future planting, the opposite of permanent ending.

options.text: Allow human political alliances to eventually restore the kingdom on their own.
options.note: The chapter has just shown such alliances failing catastrophically; the promise is explicitly God's own planting, not human diplomacy.

options.text: Restore the kingdom, but only as a low vine like the one already judged.
options.note: The image escalates beyond a low, dependent vine to a majestic, towering cedar sheltering many nations.

options.text: Plant a tender shoot on a high mountain that grows into a majestic cedar sheltering birds of every kind.
options.note: Verses 22-23 state this promise directly, God's own sovereign planting rather than human scheming.

questions: Zedekiah broke a sworn covenant for the sake of a political safety net in Egypt. Where might you be tempted to break a promise to God because a 'safer' backup plan looks more secure?
The vine bent itself toward a second source of water even though it was already planted by abundant waters. What 'second waters' are you quietly leaning on instead of trusting God's provision?
God plants His own tender shoot rather than depending on human scheming to secure a king. Where do you need to trust God's timing rather than anxiously engineering your own rescue?
The chapter ends with an invitation: 'Birds of every kind will nest under it.' How does knowing Christ's kingdom welcomes every people shape how you view those who seem furthest from it?
God says, 'I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall.' Where have you seen God overturn merely human measures of importance and status in your own story?

translationNotes.note: The two eagles are not named in the riddle itself; verses 12-17 identify the first with Babylon and, by implication, the second with Egypt, whose horses and army Zedekiah sought, verse 15.

'Made a covenant with him, putting him under oath' reflects the historical account in 2 Chronicles 36:13, where Zedekiah is said to have rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar 'though he had made him swear allegiance by God.'

'Tender sprig' translates a Hebrew word for a young, easily overlooked twig, deliberately contrasted with the 'lofty top' from which it is taken, underscoring the humble beginnings of the promised kingdom.
